_about: The length of a day in hours, from the moon's formation to now. The moon raises tides, the tides slow the spin, and the day lengthens; the moon backs away as it does. Each point [year, value, low, high]; year is the store's astronomer's year. Made by tools/curves-deep-time.py.

source.citation: Williams, G.E. (2000), Geological constraints on the Precambrian history of Earth's rotation and the Moon's orbit, Reviews of Geophysics 38, 37–59 (tidal rhythmites: about 21.9 h at 620 million years)
Meyers, S.R. & Malinverno, A. (2018), Proterozoic Milankovitch cycles and the history of the solar system, PNAS 115, 6363–6368 (18.7 h at 1.4 billion years)

Lantink, M.L., Davies, J.H.F.L., Ovtcharova, M. & Hilgen, F.J. (2022), Milankovitch cycles in banded iron formations constrain the Earth–Moon system 2.46 billion years ago, PNAS (16.9 ± 0.2 h at 2,460 million years)

Mitchell, R.N. & Kirscher, U. (2023), Mid-Proterozoic day length stalled by tidal resonance, Nature Geoscience 16, 567–569 (a day held near 19 h from about 2 to 1 billion years); disputed by Farhat, M. and others (2024), Astronomy & Astrophysics 684, A49

Wells, J.W. (1963), Coral growth and geochronometry, Nature (about 400 daily ridges a year in Middle Devonian corals, about 390 million years, range 385 to 410: 21.9 h; 385 and 390 in Pennsylvanian corals, about 300 million years: 22.6 h)
de Winter, N.J. and others (2020), a rudist shell from Oman, about 70 million years old, with 372 daily layers a year: 23.5 h
the first point, at the Moon-making impact 4,510 million years ago: models of the Moon-making impact, a day of about five hours
4,000, 3,500 and 3,000 million years: model, not measurement

howSure: Firm at the few dated points (2,460 million years, 1,400 million, 620 million, about 390 million and about 70 million); between them a judgment, with the band saying how much; before 2,500 million years a model, not a measurement, and the band is wide.
_range: from and to are the store years (astronomer's years) the curve is meaningful between — its first and last points; minPoints is the fewest points a period must hold for the curve to be offered (Prompt-Build-Timeline-Stack.md, part 6, 10 Oct 2026)
